title: Game dev tools are great at designing systems, but not running them
author: samnovakfit
selftext:
Lately I’ve been looking at a bunch of newer game dev tools, and something keeps bugging me. We’re actually pretty well covered when it comes to designing systems. There are tools for economies, level design, spreadsheets for balancing, all that stuff. It’s getting easier to think things through and prototype how a system should work. But once you move past that stage and actually have to run the system - maintain it, tweak values, ship changes safely - everything starts to fall apart a bit. In most teams I’ve seen (including ours), item data ends up scattered across spreadsheets, docs, and configs. Loot tables are easy to talk about but annoying to keep updated. Even small balance changes can take longer than they should, and over time design and engineering start drifting out of sync.   
It kind of feels like the real gap isn’t more design tools, but better ways to *operate* these systems once they exist.   
Not tools that help you answer “what should the economy look like?”  
More like tools that help you actually manage items, balancing, and live changes without everything turning into chaos.  
I'm interested how you all handle this in practice.  
Are you still mostly relying on spreadsheets + custom tooling, or have you found something that actually makes this easier?

comments.author: speaks-with-stone
comments.body:
Custom tooling, of course. For my narrative/management deterministic sim game, I built a small in-browser IDE. It's composable, everything I need a tool for gets a tool, and the whole thing is directly integrated into the game runtime. So over time design and engineering keep getting tighter and better, with faster and faster iterations. 

What is preventing your data from being organized?

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body: That actually sounds like a really nice setup,  especially having it tied directly into the runtime. For me it’s less about data not being organized and more about how things evolve over time. It usually starts clean, but as systems grow, you get quick changes, edge cases, different people touching it, and suddenly logic + data + notes are split across places. Custom tooling definitely solves that (like what you built), I guess I just keep noticing that almost every team ends up building something like this from scratch.

comments.author: pcgnlebobo
comments.body:
Same thing with asset management during dev lifecycle. Like the other poster says custom tooling is the answer. 

It's not enough to have an asset pipeline. You also need an interface and tool to manage and tweak and fine tune and integrate those assets into the game experience.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body: Having a pipeline isn’t enough on its own, you also need a way to interact with it, tweak things, and iterate without friction. Otherwise it technically “works” but slows you down every time you want to change something. Feels like items/economy systems are kind of stuck in that same spot right now.

comments.author: SplinterOfChaos
comments.body:
Typically, people will manage their spreadsheets to balance the game and then set up automation to have the game pull in the database at startup. I think I remember a dev from Reigns talk about how their database could even be updated while the game is running.

Item data should not be scattered between spreadsheets, docs, and configs, though. How'd that happen?

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body: I’ve seen setups like that too where the game pulls directly from a structured source. I think “scattered” might’ve been a bit misleading on my part. It’s usually not chaos from the start, more like it becomes fragmented over time as systems grow and more people/tools get involved. Even with a single source of truth, the workflow around editing, testing, and shipping changes can still get pretty clunky.

comments.author: Constant_Physics8504
comments.body: I actually think we don’t have all we need in systems yet, because yes we have so many things but nothing to string them together

replies.author: One_Advertising2260
replies.body: Long story short. I started vibe coding last week, im 26 and know nothing about code. The way its organized the best way to develop it. issues to keep an eye out for, the cases that fall in the cracks to resurface later, etc.. As i started branching out my program a bit i started reaching out to different places and asking what people wanted or needed or whats wrong with what does exist. Everyones response points to the same thing, you've hit it the closest so far. REAL WORRY: I genuinly feel like im making progress over here, i do...but theres that background worry of "what if it seems like its working fine but then in the end i find a terrible architecture mistake that doesnt allow this program to be what im envisioning.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body: That worry is honestly very real 😅 a lot of systems feel fine early on and only show problems once they scale. I think the good sign is that you’re already thinking about structure and asking people what’s missing, that usually helps avoid the worst cases. A lot of teams don’t get it “right” upfront anyway, they iterate into it. The tricky part is making sure your setup can evolve without turning into a mess later.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body: that’s pretty much the feeling I’ve been having. It’s not like we’re missing tools entirely, it’s more that they don’t connect into a smooth workflow once you’re actively iterating. So you end up stitching together a bunch of things instead of having something that treats it as one continuous process.

replies.author: One_Advertising2260
replies.body: THIS! it's what I'm aiming for. It's incredibly time consuming, everything becomes another problem or layer you have to add. I sent you a DM

comments.author: HealthyWest6482
comments.body:
my project has umm.. a gratuitous amount of features. (throw the table at the wall, see what sticks) that's created a massive amount of intermingling systems and balance keeping.

just off the top of my head:

10 weapon archetypes  
5 classes  
140 class skill nodes  
150 weapons  
123 armors  
473 affixes  
114 enemies  
370 events  


its overwhelming but codex is really good at reports. can compile everything you have in tables, charts, visual data. will also build simulations and calculate balance if asked. loves to write scripts for this kind of stuff to help manage the overflow. to prevent drift just keep a good set of docs.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
That scale sounds intense. I can see how that gets hard to manage quickly. Using tools to generate reports/simulations definitely helps on the analysis side. I guess where I keep seeing friction is more on the “making changes and keeping everything in sync” side, especially as things keep evolving.

Docs help a lot, but they can drift too, so it becomes this constant effort to keep everything aligned.

replies.author: HealthyWest6482
replies.body: One thing I notice is that if you task an agent to update docs, they unsurprisingly use (sometimes drifted) docs to route.  'Let's blind audit the codebase and generate a thorough report of findings - then we'll compare and trace inconsistent material with intentional practice'. If I have claude usage laying around, sometimes I'll have opus do the same thing with codex - then they peer review eachother. creates solid forward groundwork with more confidence that docs and architecture are stable.

comments.author: Trashy_io
comments.body:
I have a full folder full of a game dev workflow and any time I need to balance something I have an agent write me a balance sheet in the BalanceSheet.md I just say "I need to balance X and Z give me a chart with the stats for (A,B,C) and include Y in BalanceSheet.md" and then go make some coffee come back and its set up to usually give suggestions solutions test the best idea between mine and its and from personal feel seems to eliminate any extra guess work. 

One thing I am considering adding to that .md file is instructions to include a hidden cost section just giving things to consider before making changes to that particular balance point across different systems. 

Hope this helps also I have my workflow/set zipped up and free

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body: That’s interesting workflow. Having something generate structured balance sheets and even suggest changes sounds like it removes a lot of the manual overhead. I guess the part I’m still curious about is how that connects back into the actual game data and iteration loop,  like going from “analysis/suggestions” to “applied and tested changes” without extra friction.

replies.author: Trashy_io
replies.body: Typical I just have to manually test and for less friction I create "dev tools" that are basically just cheat codes to help me quickly test that change, Im working on putting together a (across all projects) dev tool sheet as well for the workflow as having to ask to build them out every time is definitely not as efficient, id love to be able reliably have AI test as well but typically will just say its done/corrected and when going to check it yourself it has a bug. Maybe that would be worth trying to build out!

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:

From what I’ve seen, it’s more useful on the “keeping systems and balance under control” side, not just generating ideas.
